title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A transcription service used by approximately 25 million people can automatically join virtual meetings through videoconferencing platforms without asking all participants for consent and record their conversations. The service then uses these recordings to train its AI systems. The company's privacy policy states users can consent to this through a checkbox, but the lawsuit alleges many users do not know their conversations are being shared this way or understand what happens to the recordings afterward.

The system was deployed with consent mechanisms that may not have reached all people whose speech would be captured and used. A meaningful check would have required explicit notification to and affirmative permission from every meeting participant before recording began, not just the user who installed the software. It is not established whether the company knew participants lacked knowledge of the recording, or what its de-identification process actually accomplishes.

Class-action suit claims Otter AI secretly records private work conversations
Otter.ai faces class action lawsuit for unauthorized meeting recording
Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal class-action lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a popular AI transcription service, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The suit, filed by Justin Brewer of San Jacinto, claims the company records meetings through its Otter Notebook tool and uses the audio to train its artificial intelligence systems without properly informing participants. According to the lawsuit, the software can automatically join virtual meetings through Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams without asking all attendees for consent, violating state and federal privacy laws.

Otter.ai, which serves approximately 25 million users and has processed over 1 billion meetings since 2016, claims it has permission through its privacy policy when users check a box allowing the company to use meeting transcripts for improvement purposes. However, the lawsuit argues that many users are unknowingly having their conversations shared with Otter for financial gain. The suit also raises questions about the company's ability to properly anonymize audio before using it for machine learning, noting that Otter provides no public explanation of its de-identification process.
